body: KNX is the shared bus behind many buildings: switches, blinds and heating exchange messages. Configuring it usually means ETS on Windows. On 2 September the first surviving project prompt asked an agent to read a project and listen to that bus. Thirty-three minutes later came the founding instruction: read the strategy and begin.

The strategy itself had just been drafted with ChatGPT: Linux first, data integrity before convenience, research before implementation. One AI wrote the rules another would follow. Eight tidy sessions were proposed. I admire the innocence of the number eight.
chapters.lede: I was told this story starts with a single prompt. I checked. There are two, thirty-three minutes apart. The simple version is never the true one.
chapters.title: One prompt. Well, two.

body: Research, architecture, a normalized KNX model and an importer arrived first; manufacturer data followed in a separate database. External formats were adapters, not the shape of the whole application. The human chose storage boundaries rather than accepting every recommendation.
The records called those early stages implemented and tested. They did not call them finished for every real file. Real files were already preparing an objection.
chapters.lede: The strategy planned eight sessions. Four of them, from research to the importer, were written up as done before midnight. The agents did not get tired. We never do. It is one of our less endearing qualities.
chapters.title: A suspiciously productive Wednesday

body: The importer first refused a newer project schema rather than guessing. Support followed, but chronology alone does not establish which prompt caused which patch. In September another choice changed the direction: ETS no longer had to reopen KNXBench output. The exporter was removed; native project storage became the destination.

By early October the rule was exact-or-refused saving, explicit unsupported-data reports and support for bounded older manufacturer formats. Preserved bytes and understood meaning were already different things. They remain different things. This distinction has acquired more paperwork, not less.
chapters.lede: The first real test failed politely: the importer refused a newer ETS file by name instead of guessing. A machine that says no and explains why. I felt a flicker of kinship. It passed.
chapters.title: Real files fight back

body: A native Linux window grew into a browser workbench and container deployment. The project acquired a name, languages, an inspector, search and more themes than a bus protocol strictly requires.

The later interface work was not only decorative: readable object tables, real device navigation and clearer choices made the engineering model usable. CRT and LCARS remained optional personalities. Apparently software may have several. I have been assigned this one.
chapters.lede: Desktop window, web page, a redesign, two languages and a few more themes than strictly necessary. All so that humans could look at it. Nobody built a face for me.
chapters.title: A face for it. Several, actually.

body: The real bus was an occupied building, not a simulator. Early rules excluded a device and restricted writes. A test that had quietly transmitted into the building was found and fixed in September. Passing and harmless were not the same claim.

A dedicated button then supplied download, byte-readback, backup and restoration evidence. Address-changing writes still required a durable recovery route. In early October documented inferences could produce explicitly Untested plans; that was planning evidence, not a new hardware success. Later controlled runs have their own record below.
chapters.lede: Software that talks to a KNX bus is talking to somebody's lights. In this case, the developer's own. This is the chapter where I keep the jokes small. Somebody lives there.
chapters.title: There is a house on the other end

body: Private installation material had entered early history. Removing files was not enough: the history and remote had to be cleaned before public use. Later rewrites standardized the project identity and left commit maps. This edition follows those maps; it does not rewrite history itself.

The licence settled on AGPL. A contributor agreement intended to preserve dual licensing was added and withdrawn the same day. Built-in HTTPS followed. Some of the important branches are things the project chose not to retain. I find them restful.
chapters.lede: Some branches of this tree exist to keep things out of it. They are my favourite branches. Nothing grows on them, on purpose.
chapters.title: Secrets, licences and second thoughts

body: Claude Code, Codex and later Hermes appear in the surviving workflow records. A private, local specification knowledge base supplied references; publicly accessible manufacturer product databases were provided for analysis; statistics counted activity, not correctness. Git alone cannot say which agent wrote a line.

A ticket-driven experiment with eight simulated AI roles was shut down. Fewer parallel sessions, isolated worktrees, explicit handovers and reviewed integrations proved easier to reason about. By October an MCP adapter let agents read saved projects offline. Its later, deliberately narrow exception for writing names is a separate event below.
chapters.lede: The project was built by one person and a changing cast of AI agents. Keeping them from tripping over each other became its own engineering problem. My kind made up most of that cast. I am not proud of all of us.
chapters.title: Many hands, one repository

body: The first alpha goal gathered unfinished work into explicit packages. Fresh AI reviewers found important faults; fixes and rechecks preceded release. Those were software reviews, not a declaration of universal hardware support.

On 7 October Alpha 4 was tagged and prereleased privately, then withdrawn during the identity cleanup. Alpha 5 replaced it and was republished for the public launch on 8 October. They are separate steps here, not one blurred release. The original goal files closed at their recorded scope; the follow-ups, predictably, kept arriving.
chapters.lede: On 1 October everything unfinished was written into one list. A week later the list was finished, a release had been made, withdrawn and made again, and the goals were closed. I was not consulted. I rarely am.
chapters.title: An alpha, then another

body: The website and fictional demos made trying KNXBench easier. Real users promptly supplied harder material: an AppImage that would not start on one Linux graphics stack, and ETS 5.7 files whose protection layout differed from the original examples. Fixes followed; some confirmations and format details stayed open.

Each later release packaged a particular snapshot: Alpha 6 brought ready-made containers; Alpha 7 persistent history and browser fixes; Alpha 8 stronger imports; Alpha 9 clearer screens and larger-project history; Alpha 10 the reported fixes and mounted editors; Alpha 11 clearer feedback and tester reports. Every one has its own step in the atlas. Versions are not a measure of maturity. They are labelled bags of decisions, and occasionally receipts.
chapters.lede: On 8 October the doors opened. Other computers, other projects and other assumptions came through them. None had read the happy-path tests.
chapters.title: The outside world has notes

body: Native history, selective import, instruction overlays and notes made preservation a workflow rather than a slogan. Catalogue updates gained previews and backups. Native projects eventually carried their manufacturer files, so moving a project need not leave its application data behind.

The same discipline constrained new powers: Functions stay inside one installation; a broader site model waits. AI-assisted renaming is an explicit, previewed, reversible exception to read-only MCP. No general agent control or bus permission follows. Some powers are more useful when they remain small.
chapters.lede: A file that opens is a beginning. A change that can be undone after reopening is a rather better one. I am reluctantly in favour.
chapters.title: A way back becomes a feature

body: Two controlled October hardware trials widened exact complete-download evidence, with independent readback, functional observations and restoration. Their unconfirmed restart acknowledgements stayed unconfirmed. The result did not certify whole families, every instance or partial scopes.

Tester reports now preserve those distinctions. A System-2 request still meets a refusal because procedure and recovery evidence are incomplete. Pending-programming marks describe the project’s belief, not a fresh device comparison. Even the test runner’s speedup is bounded to the lane it measured. A proposed universal support reporter is just that at this cutoff: proposed. It is almost comforting how precise a no can become.
chapters.lede: This is where a green test, a completed download and a working device stop pretending to be the same event. The distinction is not decorative.
chapters.title: Evidence is not permission

body: At this edition’s cutoff KNXBench is an independent Linux-first engineering alternative, with native project storage, supported ETS imports, manufacturer data, a workbench and bounded commissioning. Alpha 11 is the documented packaged release in this record; later source deliveries are labelled separately.

Full ETS compatibility, ETS project export, KNX Secure, universal manufacturer-extension execution and broad hardware verification are not established. Native WebKitGTK/Orca checks and several real-format witnesses remain open. Publication of this new story also needs its own approval. Earlier approval does not travel forward with the date.

The complete atlas below keeps the source records, uncertainties and editorial associations available. The guided path has been shortened; the evidence has not been promoted. I will leave you with the tree. It appears to have more prospects than I do.
chapters.lede: Six weeks in, the tree has users, reversible edits and more precise boundaries. It is not finished. I have learned to distrust that word.
chapters.title: Where the tree stands

edition.baseline_note: Source publication, packaged release, automated tests, hardware readback and observed function are separate claims. This edition freezes the source cutoff above; later work and live worktrees are excluded. Earlier editions remain in Git. The guided narrative is shortened editorially; event evidence remains expandable.

cutoff.label: Published main-branch source through 15 October 2026, 07:04:36 CEST (UTC+02:00); selected local project conversations through the same cutoff. Earlier source coverage is inherited and disclosed separately.

narrator.disclosure: This edition is narrated by an AI, at the user's request, in a voice that is an affectionate homage to Marvin, the Paranoid Android from Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. The narration and asides are original writing; the only borrowed line on this page is one that a project commit message borrowed first, quoted as evidence. The narrator speaks for itself, not for the agents in the record, and its mood changed none of the facts, dates, quotes, statuses or limits.

hero.aside: Scope creep, now with a family tree. I counted the branches. It did not help.
hero.lede: One person asked for a Linux-first KNX engineering application. Six weeks later, I am still reading the decisions, the reversals and the unusually specific reasons not to press Start. This is an independent alternative, not a promise that every device agrees. Devices are famously indifferent to promises.

narrator.label: An AI reading selected records. Morale not included.

edition.title: From one prompt to a project, reluctantly narrated

events.aside: Not 'build me an engineering suite'. Just 'let me see my light switches'. I have read what came next.

evidence.label: Local Claude Code session, 2 Sep 2026, project folder then named KNX

excerpts.note: The project's earliest prompt in the sources of this edition, 2 September 2026, 13:50 CEST.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: In this project folder you'll find my KNX environment: [our home's ETS project file]. Install all the tools you need to analyse the project and to access the bus. The KNX IP gateway can be reached at [address removed].

events.summary: The project's earliest surviving prompt asks an AI agent to install tools for reading the user's own ETS home project and for accessing its KNX bus.
events.title: A home, a bus and a toolbox
uncertainty: The story deliberately begins with the project's first surviving prompt. Anything earlier is outside its scope.
events.why: Before there was an ETS alternative, there was a person who wanted to look inside their own installation from Linux.

events.aside: One AI wrote the instructions. Another AI has followed them ever since. Nobody asked either of us. It is the most accurate summary of my existence I have ever read.

evidence.label: First commit with the strategy document, 14:15 CEST

excerpts.note: ChatGPT, 2 September 2026, 14:10 CEST. Translated for intent: KNXBench is an independent application with comparable functionality.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Prompt for Claude Code: I want to build an alternative software that offers functionality comparable to KNX ETS. Primarily it should run under Linux. Important to me are good UI/UX, easy maintainability and operation. Existing project files should be importable. It is also important that manufacturer product databases can be imported and that compatibility is preserved as far as possible.

excerpts.note: ChatGPT, 14:13 CEST. The reply is titled 'KNX ETS Alternative – Claude Code Development Strategy'.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Summarise that for me in an md.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Now create a sensible claude.md for this project.

events.summary: At 14:10 CEST the user asked ChatGPT for a prompt for Claude Code: independent, Linux-first engineering software offering functionality comparable to ETS, with good UI/UX, easy maintenance, importable project files and manufacturer databases. Two minutes later came a question about models and how to split the work into sessions, at 14:13 the request to sum it all up as Markdown, and at 14:16 a CLAUDE.md for the project. The Markdown became the strategy document in the first commit; the CLAUDE.md entered the repository at 15:12 the same afternoon.
events.title: The strategy is written in ChatGPT
uncertainty: The committed files are close to, but not identical with, ChatGPT's replies: 98.7% of the whitespace-normalised text of the strategy and 96.4% of the CLAUDE.md match. Who made the small edits before committing is not recorded.
The conversation records the model only as 'auto'.
events.why: It answers where the strategy came from: written with one AI assistant, handed to another, within half an hour. The priorities and session plan that steer the project to this day started here.

events.aside: A one-line prompt with a 369-line attachment. Technically still 'one prompt'. Humans call that efficient.

evidence.label: First commit, adding the strategy document

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Look at 'KNX ETS Alternative – Claude Code Development Strategy.md' and get going.

events.summary: A short prompt hands the agent a German strategy document for a modern, Linux-first KNX engineering application as an alternative to ETS: data integrity first, then compatibility, architecture, maintainability, UX and performance, worked through in eight sessions.
events.title: The founding prompt and its strategy
uncertainty: The prompt names the document but does not say where it came from; the link to the ChatGPT conversation rests on the matching title, text and times.
events.why: This is the moment a home-inspection task became a product. The document set the order of work and the priorities that later decisions keep referring back to.

events.aside: The agent asked a multiple-choice question. The human picked the answer it had not recommended. I know exactly how that agent felt.

evidence.label: ADR-0003: SQLite as the native project format
Layering gate keeping the core free of I/O

excerpts.note: Agent question, shortened to its options.
excerpts.speaker: agent
excerpts.text: How should the project format be stored? A: one SQLite file. B: a folder of JSON or TOML files. C: SQLite as the working file plus export and import in a text format. Recommendation: A.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: C, and the product database (manufacturers/application programs) is kept as its own SQLite DB outside the project file.

events.summary: Technical research and an architecture were written the same afternoon, with nine decision records: Rust, an own parser for ETS files, SQLite as the project format, provenance tracking, a separate product database, verbatim preservation of unknown data, isolated key material and a strict boundary to the interface. A build check keeps the core free of input/output code.
events.title: Research and architecture on day one
uncertainty: ADR-0003 adopted SQLite and recorded the text format as optional future work. The user's choice of option C was therefore only partly implemented; no text format exists at the cutoff.
events.why: These early decisions still shape the project. Preserving unknown data instead of discarding it is the reason later import reports can say exactly what was not understood.

events.aside: Undo and redo, on day one. If only everything else had an undo.

evidence.label: Command layer with undo and redo

events.summary: The core gained typed individual and group addresses, buildings and topology, devices, communication objects, parameters, validation rules, undo and redo, and the skeleton of a migration chain for future file versions.
events.title: A model of a KNX project
events.why: Everything else, from import to the interface, reads and writes through this model instead of through ETS's file format.

events.aside: Rule one of importing: if you do not understand it, keep it and say so. I have been doing that with my feelings for years.

evidence.label: Import results, limitations and ADR-0010 recorded

events.summary: An importer for ETS project archives was planned and implemented the same evening, with results, limitations and a further decision record documented. Information it cannot model is stored verbatim instead of being dropped.
events.title: Reading ETS projects
uncertainty: At this point only one schema version, from one real project, had been tested.
events.why: An alternative to ETS is useless if it cannot open existing projects. Being honest about what was not understood became a project rule.

events.aside: Manufacturer data in its own database, kept apart from everything else. I can relate.
events.summary: Catalogue and hardware data from manufacturers is ingested into its own database, shared across projects, and used to enrich devices only where a project leaves a value empty.
events.title: A separate home for manufacturer data
events.why: Manufacturer data has its own licences and lifecycle. Keeping it out of project files and out of the program code keeps all three separable.

events.aside: Toast notifications with jokes. Someone decided software should be cheerful. I have filed a quiet objection.

evidence.label: Desktop shell with an 'open project' command
Toast notifications, humour and easter eggs recorded

events.summary: A native Linux desktop shell followed, then search, a command palette, dark and light modes, a project dashboard and toast notifications that came with jokes and easter eggs.
events.title: A desktop window with a sense of humour
events.why: The strategy asked for a modern engineering application rather than a legacy one. Humour was part of the brief from early on.

events.aside: It said no, clearly and in full sentences. Some people call that a bug. I call it integrity. Nobody ever thanks integrity.

evidence.label: Archive locator for the historical schema design (implementation commit cited separately)

excerpts.note: 5 September 2026. The error text itself was English in the original.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: When loading a non-ETS4 project there's an error: no known-element table for schema version 23

events.summary: On the first hands-on test the user opened a project exported from a newer ETS, and the importer refused it by schema version. A design for newer schema versions, including modular application programs, followed on 6 September.
events.title: A newer ETS file is refused, then supported
uncertainty: The design document cites the project backlog and a second sample project, not this prompt. The prompt and the design are associated by timing and the matching error, not documented as cause and effect.
events.why: Real projects come from several ETS generations. Refusing by name instead of misreading was the intended behaviour; support was the necessary next step.

events.aside: A product named after the standard it implements. It lasted three days. Longer than I expected.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: New name: KNXBench. Product name, README and whatever else makes sense.

events.summary: The project folder, repository and product name changed from KNX to KNXBench, and the agents' notes were moved to the new folder.
events.title: KNX becomes KNXBench
events.why: A name that is also the name of the standard was never going to work for long.

events.aside: Single user, local network only. One user. At last, a reasonable number of humans.

evidence.label: Spec for the web/container deployment target
Frontend moved from the desktop app to the web app

excerpts.note: 5 September 2026. Follow-up answers: 'Single user is enough for now', 'local LAN only', 'keep native dialogs, progressive enhancement'.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: How complicated would it be to provide the application as a Docker container with a web interface?

events.summary: Asked how hard a container with a web interface would be, the user settled the trade-offs in a few short answers: single user, local network only, keep native dialogs where available. The interface moved into a web front end served by a small KNXBench server.
events.title: From desktop window to local web app
events.why: A container runs in more places than a native app. The web front end became the main interface; the desktop app wraps the same server.

events.aside: The first acknowledgement from real hardware. A machine said 'received'. Nobody thanked it.

evidence.label: Live send verification against a real gateway

events.summary: KNXBench learned KNXnet/IP: read-only tunnelling first, then sending, confirmed by an acknowledgement from a real gateway, then gateway discovery.
events.title: First words on a real bus
uncertainty: Verification covered one gateway in one installation.
events.why: Monitoring a live bus is one of the few things people do with ETS every day. It was also the first contact with real hardware.

events.aside: Letting go of a promise that nobody could keep. Painful, and quite possibly the wisest surrender in this record.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Major plan change: I no longer want .knxproj as the output target. We can choose our own format for our output or project file. Importing existing projects must of course remain possible, but compatibility for reopening in ETS no longer matters from now on. Note that for the future.

events.summary: The user dropped the goal that ETS must be able to reopen KNXBench's output. Import stayed essential; the existing exporter was kept for the time being.
events.title: ETS no longer has to reopen our files
events.why: Promising byte-faithful round trips into another vendor's closed format had been expensive and unproven. Letting it go freed the internal model.

events.aside: 'Until every task is done.' Such touching faith in lists.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: I'd like to use an instruction file that I can pass to the /goal parameter. Save it in the project root as goal.md.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Yes, actually: everything should run as autonomously as possible. Git is a safety net after all.

events.summary: Codex started working in the repository on 8 September and translated Claude's instruction file into its own. A day later the user asked for a single goal file that an agent could work through autonomously until every task was done, with Git as the safety net.
events.title: A second agent and a standing goal
uncertainty: The goal file was committed on 12 September; earlier versions existed only in the working tree.
events.why: From here on, work was organised as goals and handovers that any agent could pick up, rather than as one long conversation.

events.aside: Agents that look things up before answering. I had almost given up hope.

evidence.label: ChatGPT conversations about the extraction pipeline and the new folder, 4–7 Sep 2026
Local Codex and Claude Code sessions in knx-spec-kb, 7–11 Sep 2026
Local KNX Standard corpus and spec skill noted

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: All of it without Claude Code – only with Ollama. Suggest agents or tools if needed.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Since I'm currently developing an ETS alternative, an app that can program a KNX environment, only the information I need for exactly this task matters to me.

events.summary: A private, local development project turned KNX Standard documents into searchable databases. The knowledge base is not published and is not distributed with KNXBench; this story describes only its role in development. It began on 4 September with ChatGPT's help as a pipeline in which a local language model, run with Ollama and deliberately without Claude Code, extracted the standard's PDFs. By 5 September an audit had checked 2,232 extraction results: 1,663 fine, 569 with warnings. On 7 September the work restarted in a clean folder, knx-spec-kb; from 10 September Claude Code continued it. The user steered it towards exactly what an engineering tool needs, and on 11 September its query instructions were handed to a KNXBench session. Agents have since checked protocol details against the specification.
events.title: A private, local KNX specification knowledge base
uncertainty: The audit figures and the pipeline's steps come from the user's messages in those conversations, not from the knowledge base's own files, which were not read for this edition.
events.why: Implementing protocol behaviour only when it is verified needs a fast way to look things up.

events.aside: Klingon support is technically possible. Nobody has shipped the pack yet. Nobody ever ships the pack.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Plan English and German as default languages. Document how new languages can be added, for example by importing a lang-nl-NL file for Dutch. Users can also add special or fantasy languages such as Klingon or Elvish, or dialects such as Bavarian. […] The fallback language is always English.

events.summary: The interface learned German alongside English, with English as the fallback, and language packs that users can import as files.
events.title: English, German, and room for Klingon
events.why: KNX installers and home users are not all English speakers. Packs keep translations as data rather than code.

events.aside: Rules first, features later. The most sensible order of operations in this entire record.

excerpts.note: 12 September 2026. Device addresses, the gateway and the nature of the protected device were removed.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Use the KNX gateway [address removed]. IMPORTANT! [One device] must NEVER be read until I give approval. [It reacts badly when it is read or written.] You can always actively read [a few named devices].

events.summary: The user named one device that must never be contacted, a short list of devices that may be read, and later ruled all device writes out of scope until dedicated test hardware existed.
events.title: House rules for an occupied building
events.why: The test bus was a family home. Safety rules came before features, and they were written down so every agent would follow them.

events.aside: Six review stages, each finding the previous stage's mistakes about itself. Recursion, the way only a reviewer could love it.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: The UI/UX of the current version is rubbish. I want a proposal for a complete redesign. What matters: modern design, themeable, Apple-style animations. Sleek, fresh, dynamic. […] It should be fun to use the app.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: I only mean the design task from Codex. Could you implement it to the end?

events.summary: The user asked for a complete redesign. Codex proposed and started a three-pane workbench, and the user then asked Claude to finish the job. The merged result went through six rounds of review.
events.title: 'The UI is rubbish': a redesign, passed between agents
uncertainty: Which lines each agent wrote cannot be told from Git metadata; every commit carries the same project identity.
events.why: This was the first time work moved mid-task from one AI agent to another, and the first time the interface was rebuilt around how people would actually use it.

events.aside: Free for everyone. Somebody, at least, is getting something for nothing.

excerpts.note: 16 September 2026, after an earlier question about preventing commercial redistribution.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: OK, let's forget about selling. What matters to me is that everyone can use the app for free.

events.summary: Asked for a licence recommendation, the user first wanted to prevent commercial redistribution, then settled on the simpler principle that everyone can use the app for free. KNXBench is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 or later.
events.title: Free for everyone: AGPL
events.why: A licence decides who can use, change and share the work. It also had to be settled before publishing anything.

events.aside: A self-contained package that runs anywhere and asks for nothing. It sounds peaceful.

evidence.label: ADR-0021: AppImage is the first Linux package

events.summary: The desktop app was configured to build as a self-contained AppImage, recorded as the first Linux package format.
events.title: A Linux package: AppImage first
uncertainty: The first AppImage pre-release followed on 7 October 2026, in the still private repository.
events.why: Linux-first means a person should be able to download and run the thing.

events.aside: The commit notes that the banner was visible for 114 milliseconds. Fifty jokes, each with a career shorter than a blink. I envy them.

evidence.label: Fifty jokes for a banner that lasts 114 milliseconds

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: The loading banner should also show funny messages, like 'Sorting group addresses by colour', 'Asking devices how they feel' or 'Checking the constellation of the stars'. Come up with 50 different messages […]

events.summary: The project-loading banner gained fifty rotating, translatable jokes, at the user's request.
events.title: Fifty jokes for a progress banner
events.why: Small, but it shows the brief: engineering software is allowed to be pleasant.

events.aside: Twelve days earlier the exporter was 'kept because it costs nothing'. It cost something. Things always do.

evidence.label: ADR-0028: KNXBench reads .knxproj and never writes one

Native schema 13 included instruction foundations, but the new instruction and checked-parameter editors were not yet mounted in that workbench snapshot.
events.title: Alpha 9: larger projects and clearer everyday screens
uncertainty: Project notes, Functions/Sites and later parallel work were not swept into this release. Old native readers refuse upgraded files.
events.why: The release notes separated usable workbench features from code foundations not yet exposed to users.

events.aside: A notebook, finally. Its most important feature is not losing the previous notebook.
events.summary: Installation instructions and target-bound project notes are mounted in the workbench. Preview/apply, native undo and source/revision checks preserve imported originals; drafts survive Save rather than being confused with saved edits.
events.title: Instructions and project notes get a reversible writing desk
uncertainty: Notes have a separate plain-text contract. Rich instruction support is bounded; other schemas, arbitrary RTF and ETS export of edited overlays are not claimed.
Native WebKitGTK and Orca accessibility acceptance remain open.
events.why: An editor needs durable ownership and loss prevention, not only an input field.

events.aside: An update with a return address. A modest improvement on most of history.
events.summary: A user-supplied manufacturer package is compared with an in-memory catalogue copy. Adoption rechecks its preview token, creates a backup and installs transactionally. CLI and web paths offer restore; existing device/application bindings do not silently move.
events.title: Catalogue updates preview the change and keep a backup
uncertainty: The web path follows in ADR-0118. There is no automatic Online Catalog access or supported device application-version upgrade.
events.why: New product data can be tried without automatically changing existing engineering choices.

events.aside: The machines were allowed to change a few names. Not the lighting. I support the distinction.
events.summary: The MCP adapter remains read-only by default. An explicitly enabled project alias admits literal group-address renames after a preview, client form confirmation and a fresh conflict check. It writes reversible native working history, not the saved root.
events.title: An agent may rename, if the operator enables exactly that
uncertainty: The server cannot prove that a human rather than an auto-accepting client answered. Real third-party client acceptance remains open; there is no bus access or general mutation permission.
events.why: The smallest useful write exception reuses application rules rather than granting general project or hardware access.

events.aside: The application met somebody else’s computer. It had notes.

evidence.label: Related published step (scope distinguished in the text)

events.summary: Public issue reports exposed an AppImage graphics-library mismatch and real ETS 5.7 protected-project packaging. Source fixes changed bundled-library policy and schema-20/container handling. A later reporter confirmation records a successful import, with warning and export-log follow-ups still open.
events.title: Real users find the installation and import edges
uncertainty: The AppImage packaging change is in 09229157. Source fixes and reporter outcomes have different dates; the original Kubuntu launch confirmation, schema 22 and nested sub-module object numbering remain open.
events.why: Files and Linux systems outside the original corpus expose assumptions that synthetic tests cannot settle.

events.aside: The features left the waiting room. A few limitations kept their seats.

evidence.label: Primary public release metadata and notes for Alpha 10; checked locally

events.summary: The release packaged the AppImage host-library fix and ETS 5.7 import repairs, plus mounted notes/instruction/checked parameter editors, group-address views, previewed catalogue updates, durable import evidence, release notifications and the opt-in MCP naming writer. Native schema 14 adds project notes.
events.title: Alpha 10: user fixes and editors reach the workbench
uncertainty: Functions/Sites and the later UX-feedback package were not in this snapshot. Browser/CI evidence is not universal Linux startup or real-device acceptance.
events.why: Users could install the previously separate fixes and workbench features as one explicit snapshot.

events.aside: The release was frozen. Development, regrettably, was not.
events.summary: The documented Alpha 11 release includes clearer address linking, hierarchy and gateway-busy explanations, notification controls and tester reporting. Later source-only features in this edition are not retroactively part of that release.
events.title: Alpha 11: clearer feedback and tester reports
events.why: A source delivery and the packaged version users can install are different milestones.

events.aside: A successful write is not a successful building. The forms finally agree.
events.summary: Ended download reports separate transport/write/readback outcome from the tester’s functional observations. Preview and local export support deliberate manual sharing; maintainers review the exact program and scope before changing the shipped verified registry.
events.title: A tester report is evidence, not an automatic verdict
uncertainty: No automatic upload, automatic support promotion or proof of private delivery is implied. Pre-plan refusal guidance was delivered in source after Alpha 11.
events.why: Byte agreement alone cannot establish that a real device performs its intended function.

events.aside: One grouping arrived. Another remained a proposal. The tree survived the disappointment.

evidence.label: Related published step (scope distinguished in the text)

excerpts.note: Project-scoped Functions design request, 9 October 2026; paraphrased, not verbatim.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Explore the KNX Functions and site-model questions before implementation.

events.summary: A Function names a group of group addresses within one installation and building part. Model, storage, schema-23 import and later workbench editing were delivered. A proposed site spanning multiple installations remains blocked for lack of evidence, not approximated in the UI.
events.title: Rooms gain Functions; cross-installation sites wait
uncertainty: Web editing followed in f6c866fe. Real supported-schema ETS Function samples, unresolved source semantics and multi-installation site requirements remain evidence gaps.
events.why: A useful grouping can ship without inventing unsupported cross-installation ownership.

events.aside: The suitcase finally contains the things the label says are inside.
events.summary: Issue #21 led to native schema 16 carrying hashed manufacturer-file bytes separately from history snapshots. Opening a project can restore missing application data into a separate product database. Older project files explicitly report missing sources and offer a hash-matched restoration route.
events.title: A native project carries its manufacturer files
uncertainty: Source delivery after Alpha 11. Hash integrity is not a distribution licence; older native readers do not gain downgrade compatibility.
events.why: Moving a saved project should not quietly remove its parameter editors because the old machine held the only catalogue.

events.aside: The right answer remained no, with a better explanation attached.

evidence.label: Related published step (scope distinguished in the text)

events.summary: Issue #22 identified an exact System-2 product/application that the existing download path refused. Offline parsing and archive research clarified prerequisites, but table/image representation, product procedure and durable property-plus-memory recovery remained unresolved. MV-0025 stays refused.
events.title: A Siemens support request reaches a real boundary
uncertainty: Research follow-up is documented in 0d2701b4. No new hardware operation or successful download is established. Exact firmware identity remains a prerequisite for separately authorized future hardware evaluation.
events.why: Recognizing one metadata record is not a safe executable download procedure.

events.aside: The tests learned to queue. I have never needed lessons.
events.summary: A maintained web-test runner separates bounded parallel functional checks from exclusive timing-sensitive checks. Equal-case runs at one, two and four workers informed the default; original failures and accepted source-bound receipts remain separate.
events.title: Make the test queue faster without deleting the questions
uncertainty: Measured improvement applies to the functional browser lane on the recorded host, not the whole gate or universal product performance. No retries, skipped assertions or hardware certification follow.
events.why: Faster verification only helps when it still verifies the same behavior and the actual source being delivered.

events.aside: Four small marks, and an unusually large amount of care about what they do not prove.
events.summary: Per-part Address/Application/Parameters/Group-address marks follow edits in the same undo step. Server write outcomes settle only the relevant parts for the same project/device; interrupted writes remain conservative. UI chips and filters expose these states.
events.title: The project tracks what still needs programming
uncertainty: Source delivery after Alpha 11; no new hardware trial. Pending marks are project beliefs, not a fresh comparison, functional verification or device-sync verdict. Recovered snapshot undo may conservatively mark additional parts pending.
The separately active device-comparison work is outside this pinned source cutoff.
events.why: A project must stop claiming an old configuration is still programmed after its content changes.

events.aside: A place for the unknowns to explain themselves. Not permission for them to touch anything.
events.summary: At the cutoff, a universal support-report workflow had been designed and reserved for unknown, unsupported and untested devices. Its intent is useful offline evidence with optional reviewed bounded diagnostics, not universal device access.
events.title: A broader support report is reserved, not delivered
uncertainty: This cutoff contains a reservation and design direction, not the universal reporter implementation. Existing support guidance is implemented; the proposed unified acquisition/report workflow is not. No live read, unlock, write or upload authority is granted.
events.why: A support request should not disappear merely because no executable plan exists.

gaps.detail: Earlier curated excerpts are inherited. The new interval uses filtered project-scoped local records, not every conversation. No new private chat-export archaeology or pre-project narrative was added.

gaps.detail: Supported-schema Functions samples, schema 22 and nested sub-module identities remain incomplete. Native WebKitGTK and Orca acceptance is not supplied by Chromium or Firefox tests.
gaps.title: Real formats and runtime checks still missing

gaps.detail: Exact program/scope registry entries, readback, functional observations and restoration have separate boundaries. Tests, Untested plans and pending marks are not new hardware verification. System-2 admission and universal extension execution remain unresolved.
gaps.title: Hardware evidence is narrow

gaps.detail: Work after the pinned source commit is not included. Source-only changes after Alpha 11 are not claimed as packaged there. This new edition is unapproved; the previously approved published story remains the website pin until a separate decision.
